title: What could RED IV mean for Europe’s renewable hydrogen market?
gist: A leaked September 2026 draft impact assessment for the EU's RED IV suggests post-2030 renewable hydrogen support may shift from binding national RFNBO quotas to an indicative 2040 EU-level target, wider eligibility (incl. low-carbon hydrogen) and more member-state implementation. Wood Mackenzie argues the key risk is whether looser rules still deliver bankable, predictable demand for projects.

themes.theme: RED IV shift from binding quotas to indicative targets

insights.claim: A draft impact assessment for the EU's fourth Renewable Energy Directive (RED IV), leaked in September 2026, indicates the European Commission is considering a different approach to hydrogen from that established under RED III.
insights.speaker: Monica Trilho
insights.so_what: Post-2030 EU hydrogen demand rules are being reopened; current project business cases built on RED III could be repriced.

insights.claim: For industry and refining, the leaked RED IV draft considers replacing binding national RFNBO requirements with an indicative EU-level hydrogen target for 2040.
insights.speaker: Monica Trilho
insights.so_what: Loss of a binding industrial mandate removes the main compliance-driven demand pull for EU green hydrogen offtake.
insights.quote: the draft considers moving towards an indicative EU-level hydrogen target for 2040
insights.locator: For industry and refining, the change

insights.claim: In transport, the leaked RED IV draft would keep obligations on fuel suppliers but shift implementation increasingly to member-state level rather than a standalone EU-wide quota.
insights.speaker: Monica Trilho
insights.so_what: Transport hydrogen demand would fragment into 27 national regimes, raising policy-risk dispersion across markets.
insights.locator: In transport, obligations on fuel suppliers

insights.claim: The RED IV proposals contemplate broadening the types of hydrogen and electricity sources eligible for compliance, potentially including additional forms of low-carbon hydrogen.
insights.speaker: Monica Trilho
insights.so_what: Wider eligibility (e.g. low-carbon/blue hydrogen) dilutes the premium that RFNBO-compliant green hydrogen projects were counting on.
insights.locator: In transport, obligations on fuel suppliers

insights.claim: A binding mandate creates a clearer compliance-driven source of demand, whereas an indicative target shifts the burden onto the policies, incentives and market mechanisms used to turn ambition into actual hydrogen consumption.
insights.speaker: Monica Trilho
insights.so_what: Under an indicative regime, investors must underwrite national subsidy and incentive design rather than an EU legal obligation.
insights.quote: A binding mandate creates a clearer compliance-driven source of demand.

insights.claim: The leaked RED IV document is not adopted policy; the Commission must still publish a legislative proposal, after which the European Parliament and Council will negotiate the final framework.
insights.speaker: Monica Trilho
insights.so_what: Regulatory uncertainty on EU hydrogen demand will persist for multiple legislative stages, delaying FIDs.
insights.locator: The document is not adopted policy.

insights.claim: Renewable hydrogen in Europe has faced persistent challenges around production economics, infrastructure development and demand creation, making market development slower and more uncertain than earlier EU ambitions implied.

insights.claim: The mechanisms beneath EU hydrogen targets — national implementation, incentives, compliance rules and the interaction between transport, industrial and refining demand — could materially affect hydrogen project economics.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie flags three questions to watch as RED IV develops: how Europe creates durable hydrogen demand if binding mandates are reduced, how industrial, refining and transport demand interact, and whether incentives and compliance mechanisms provide enough certainty for project development.
